title: Foraging jack-by-the-hedge in UK hedgerows
subtitle: Garlic mustard: identification, harvest, and uses
excerpt: Jack-by-the-hedge lines UK hedgerows and woodland edges from February through June. The young leaves taste of mild garlic and raw mustard and add bite to salads and green sauces. Pick before the plant flowers for the best flavour.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); BSBI species accounts for Alliaria petiolata; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.

content.text: Jack-by-the-hedge (Alliaria petiolata), also called garlic mustard, lines UK hedgerows, roadside verges, and woodland edges from February through June. The young leaves taste of mild garlic and raw mustard, and add bite to salads, green sauces, and pestos. Pick before the plant flowers for the best flavour; the leaves become more bitter after flowering. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification
: confirm (1) a mild garlic smell when a leaf is crushed, (2) the kidney-shaped, coarsely toothed leaf, and (3) the hedgerow or woodland-edge habitat. All three must match.
ID features
Early leaves (February to March): kidney-shaped, bright green, coarsely toothed edge, around 3 to 8 cm across.
Mature leaves (April onward): heart-shaped, more triangular. The plant grows a single upright stem reaching 0.5 to 1 m.
Scent: crush a leaf; a mild garlic smell. Fainter than wild garlic but distinct.
Flowers (April to June): small, white, four-petalled, in clusters at the top of the stem. Cross-shaped, typical of the mustard family.
Poisonous look-alikes
Jack-by-the-hedge has limited toxic
look-alike plants
in the UK, but two situations cause confusion.
Lords and ladies (Arum maculatum): similar broad, toothed leaf but with dark spots or blotches, an arrow-head shape, and no garlic scent. Highly irritating; toxic if eaten.
Black bryony (Tamus communis): a climbing hedgerow plant with heart-shaped leaves but a shiny surface, no garlic scent, and red berries in autumn. Toxic.
When and how to harvest

Pick from February through April, before the plant flowers. Young leaves from the base of the plant are the most tender. Snap or snip individual leaves; do not pull the whole plant. The young leaves need no cooking and can go straight into salads. From May onward the flavour sharpens to bitter; these older leaves are better cooked briefly to reduce bitterness.
After harvesting

Rinse in cold water and use the same day. The leaves do not store well once picked. Young leaves go into salads with a simple dressing, into green sauces alongside wild garlic, or into sandwiches as a peppery leaf. The roots taste of horseradish but the plant is biennial; do not uproot it.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of foliage from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Uprooting is an offence.

rows.symptom: Leaf has no garlic scent when crushed
rows.cause: The plant may be lords and ladies or another non-garlic hedgerow plant
rows.fix: Do not eat without the scent confirmation. Lords and ladies has a similar leaf shape but is toxic and has no garlic smell.

rows.symptom: Leaves taste very bitter even from young plants
rows.cause: Older leaves or the plant is stressed or late in the season
rows.fix: Pick from the base of the plant where the youngest leaves are. If the plant has already flowered, the leaves will be unpleasantly bitter; move to a younger patch.
